# USCGC Dione

USCGC Dione (WPC-107) was a **Thetis-class patrol boat** (also classified as Argo-class) operated by the United States Coast Guard from 1934 to 1963 . The vessel was named after Dione, a Greek titaness . Commissioned in October 1934, Dione served during World War II and the Cold War before being decommissioned in 1963 and sold for commercial service .

## 1. Construction and Design

### 1.1 Design and Construction

USCGC Dione was built by the Manitowoc Shipbuilding Corporation in Manitowoc, Wisconsin . Her keel was laid down on November 10, 1933, and she was launched on June 30, 1934 . The vessel was sponsored by Unita Risch and was delivered to the Coast Guard on September 28, 1934 . Dione was commissioned on October 5, 1934, departing Manitowoc the same day .

The construction cost was \$258,000 . The vessel had a building number of P-13 and hull number 277 . Initially designated as P-13 when assigned in 1934, her designation was changed to WPC-107 in 1942 . Her signal letters were NRGV .

### 1.2 Technical Specifications

USCGC Dione had a **length overall of 165 feet (50 m)**, a length between perpendiculars of 160 feet (49 m), a maximum beam of 25 feet 3 inches (7.70 m), and a beam at the waterline of 23 feet 9 inches (7.24 m) . Her draft was 7 feet 8 inches (2 m) when constructed in 1933, and her displacement was 337 long tons (342 tonnes) when fully loaded .

The vessel had a complement of 5 officers and 39 men during its initial construction . The hull was constructed of steel and had two decks: the main deck and berth deck . The berth deck was subdivided into compartments by six transverse watertight bulkheads .

Propulsion was provided by two Winton 6-cylinder, 4-stroke diesel engines, each producing 670 brake horsepower (500 kW) for a total of 1,340 brake horsepower (1,000 kW) . These engines drove two three-bladed propellers, giving the vessel a maximum speed of 16 knots (30 km/h; 18 mph), a maximum sustained speed of 14 knots (26 km/h; 16 mph), a cruising speed of 11 knots (20 km/h; 13 mph), and an economic speed of 6 knots (11 km/h; 6.9 mph) .

The vessel's fuel capacity was 7,700 U.S. gallons (29,000 L) of diesel fuel . Dione carried two 19-foot (5.8 m) dories for boat operations .

### 1.3 Armament and Systems

The original armament of USCGC Dione upon construction included one 3-inch/23-caliber gun and two 1-pound (0.45 kg) guns . The vessel was also equipped with wireless telegraphy and World War I-era sonar systems .

In 1941 or 1942, the vessel underwent a rearmament that removed one of the 1-pound guns and added two depth charge tracks and one Y-gun .

After a major refit in 1945, Dione's armament was significantly upgraded. The 3-inch/23-caliber gun was replaced with two single-mount 3-inch/50-caliber guns . The vessel also received two single-mount 20 mm/80 cannons, two "mousetrap" anti-submarine rocket launchers, and an additional Y-gun . Her wireless set and World War I-era sonar were replaced with an SF radar system and a QCN-1 sonar system .

As a result of the 1945 refit, the vessel's displacement increased to 350 long tons (360 t), her draft increased to 10 feet (3 m), and her complement was increased to 7 officers and 68 men .

## 2. Coast Guard Service

### 2.1 Pre-War Service (1934-1941)

Following her commissioning in October 1934, USCGC Dione began her service with the Coast Guard . Prohibition had been repealed in December 1933, so the cutter was not used for anti-rum running duties as originally intended . Instead, Dione conducted search and rescue operations .

The vessel was initially homeported in Norfolk, Virginia from 1934 to 1943 . In December 1943, she was transferred to Tompkinsville, Staten Island, where she remained based until December 1944 . Tompkinsville was the site of an Eastern Sea Frontier base .

### 2.2 World War II Service (1941-1945)

Following the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, the United States entered World War II. On November 1, 1941, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8929, which transferred control of the Coast Guard from the Department of the Treasury to the Navy "for the duration of the emergency" .

#### 2.2.1 Early War Operations

During the early months of the war, USCGC Dione was assigned to both the Fifth Naval District, which contained the waters off Virginia and North Carolina, and the Eastern Sea Frontier, a Navy operational command .

One of Dione's most significant early war actions occurred on March 15, 1942, when she received a distress signal from the oil tanker Australia . The vessel rescued the crew of the storage tanker Acme early in the morning of March 18, 1942 .

#### 2.2.2 Torpedo Junction Operations

During the critical period known as "Torpedo Junction" or "Torpedo Alley," USCGC Dione played a crucial role in coastal defense . German U-boats were wreaking havoc on Allied shipping along the American East Coast during what became known as Operation Paukenschlag (Operation Drumbeat) .

According to historical accounts, **USCGC Dione was the only ship patrolling the entire region** during part of this period . Other ships had been stationed elsewhere, and they were not equipped for anti-submarine patrols . This inadequate defense contributed to what German submarine commanders referred to as "American shooting season" .

From January to June 1942, German U-boats sank 397 Allied vessels in Torpedo Junction, while American forces were only able to sink three U-boats during this timeframe . The losses eventually prompted naval leadership to take action, implementing convoy systems and deploying additional anti-submarine assets .

#### 2.2.3 Axtell J. Byles Incident

On April 19, 1942, USCGC Dione was escorting a convoy that included the unarmed oil tanker Axtell J. Byles . The convoy consisted of seven tankers and one freighter, escorted by Dione, four small US Coast Guard boats, and an aircraft . They steamed at 9.5 knots but did not zigzag .

At 00:34 hours, U-136 fired a spread of four torpedoes at the convoy about four miles off Wimble Shoals, North Carolina . A Navy aircraft spotted the incoming torpedo and warned the ships . The torpedo missed Dione by about 20 yards but struck the Axtell J. Byles at 20:00 hours, which sank shortly thereafter .

Dione dropped eight depth charges over the course of two runs in response to the attack . The vessel began patrolling around the Wimble Shoals buoy after her escort missions were finished, beginning demolition exercises on the wreck of the Axtell J. Byles on April 25 . She continued dropping depth charges for the next few days .

#### 2.2.4 Later War Operations

After the Axtell J. Byles incident, Dione continued her escort duties. The convoys began to run at night following the loss of the tanker . On April 29, Dione was ordered back to Little Creek for repairs and rearmament .

The repairs were completed on May 13, 1942 . Dione was listed as a convoy escort unit and conducted escort duty in the North Atlantic Ocean, escorting HK convoys going from New York to Key West and KN convoys heading from Key West to New York .

In 1945, Dione underwent a major refit that significantly upgraded her armament and systems . Following this refit, she was selected as one of six patrol vessels to serve as the Navy's "surrender group" for the First Naval District off New England, serving alongside her sister ships Argo and Nemesis .

On May 17, 1945, Dione rendezvoused with U-1228, a U-boat that had fled to Allied waters following the German surrender . The vessel escorted the submarine to Portsmouth, New Hampshire .

### 2.3 Post-War Service (1945-1947)

After World War II ended, the Coast Guard's jurisdiction was returned to the Department of the Treasury on January 1, 1946, via Executive Order 9666, signed by President Harry S. Truman .

From 1945 to 1947, Dione was used by the Coast Guard for law enforcement and search and rescue operations . The vessel was eventually decommissioned on July 23, 1947, in Cape May, New Jersey . She spent several years laid up in storage due to a lack of personnel .

### 2.4 Cold War Service (1951-1963)

USCGC Dione was recommissioned on February 4, 1951, in Curtis Bay, Maryland, after a shakedown cruise in the Caribbean . Starting in 1952, Dione was assigned to the Eighth Coast Guard District and based in Freeport, Texas . She was the first cutter to be based in the city .

During her Cold War service, Dione operated in various locations including Cuba, the Atlantic Ocean, New York, and Baltimore, Maryland . Personnel who served aboard Dione during this period included James Eldon Wheeler, who reached the rank of Boatswain's Mate Second Class .

One notable commanding officer during this period was Commander John E. Wesler, who served as both Executive Officer and Commanding Officer of USCGC Dione (WPC-107) . Commander Wesler was a 1949 graduate of the U.S. Coast Guard Academy who later earned master's degrees in Acoustics from MIT and Optics from the University of Rochester .

The vessel was decommissioned for the final time on February 8, 1963 . Her custody was transferred to the Texas Group of the Atlantic Reserve Fleet—the Atlantic Reserve Fleet, Orange—that same day .

## 3. Commercial Service

Following her decommissioning, USCGC Dione was sold as a supply ship on February 24, 1964 . She entered commercial service with several name changes and owners over the years .

### 3.1 Early Commercial Career (1964-1969)

Initially, the vessel was owned by the Palmer Decker Boat Company and registered in Port Arthur, Texas . She carried the official number 297193 and the call sign WD 4627 .

In March 1967, the Palmer Decker Boat Company was dissolved following a liquidation agreement unanimously executed by the company's shareholders . The ship was seized by a U.S. Marshal in September 1967 after foreclosure proceedings were filed against the company .

The vessel was sold at a court auction on December 7, 1967, to Big Trouble Inc. . It was renamed "Big Trouble" from December 1967 to February 1969 .

In February 1969, the vessel was sold to Delta Boats Inc. and renamed "Delta I" . In March 1969, under the name Delta I, she was sold from Delta Boats to Sabik Inc., still registered in New Orleans .

### 3.2 Later Commercial Operations (1969-1992)

On April 5, 1969, while operating as a geophysical exploration ship named Delta I, the vessel caught fire while traveling from Kingston, Jamaica, to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago . She was bound for the Persian Gulf .

After repairs, the vessel was rebuilt in Tampa, Florida, completed by March 1970 . She was capable of serving as "an oil rig tender, a crew boat, buoy tender, repair ship with sand blast capacity, and a line-handling vessel for super tankers" .

In late 1969, the vessel was renamed "Al Rashid" and continued in commercial service until 1992 . As Al Rashid, she had an IMO number of 7515080 .

### 3.3 Specifications as a Commercial Vessel

As a commercial vessel, the former USCGC Dione had the following specifications :

* Length: 154.3 feet (47 m)

* Beam: 25.3 feet (7.7 m)

* Draft: 11.3 feet (3.4 m)

* Gross Register Tonnage: 256 GRT

* Net Register Tonnage: 174 NRT

The vessel's final fate is unknown, as she was last seen in 1992 .

## 4. Legacy and Notability

USCGC Dione had a **29-year career** in the Coast Guard, serving during two major conflicts: World War II and the Cold War . Her service highlights include:

1. **Early Cold War Service**: Operating in Cuba and other strategic locations during the early years of the Cold War .

2. **World War II Escort Duty**: Serving as an escort vessel during the critical Battle of the Atlantic, protecting convoys along the American East Coast and in the North Atlantic .

3. **Torpedo Junction Defense**: Being the sole patrol vessel for a significant portion of the American East Coast during the early months of the U-boat campaign, a period that saw devastating losses to Allied shipping .

4. **Search and Rescue Operations**: Conducting numerous rescue missions, including the rescue of the crew of the storage tanker Acme on March 18, 1942 .

5. **Surrender Group Service**: Serving as part of the Navy's "surrender group" following Germany's surrender in 1945, including the escort of U-1228 to Portsmouth, New Hampshire .

6. **First Cutter in Freeport**: Being the first Coast Guard cutter based in Freeport, Texas, establishing a long-term presence in the city .

## 5. Commanding Officers

While comprehensive records of all commanding officers are not available in the sources, several notable officers served aboard USCGC Dione:

* **Commander John E. Wesler**: Served as both Executive Officer and Commanding Officer of USCGC Dione (WPC-107). A 1949 Coast Guard Academy graduate with advanced degrees in Acoustics and Optics .

* **Various Officers During WWII**: Including those who commanded the vessel during her critical escort and patrol duties in the Atlantic and along the East Coast .

* **Cold War Commanders**: Officers who led the vessel during her service in Cuba and other Cold War operations .

## 6. Technical Evolution

USCGC Dione underwent several significant technical changes during her service life:

1. **1941/1942 Rearmament**: Removed one 1-pound gun and added depth charge tracks and a Y-gun .

2. **1945 Major Refit**: A comprehensive upgrade that included new radar and sonar systems, upgraded armament including 3-inch/50-caliber guns and 20 mm cannons, and increased displacement and crew complement .

3. **From Prohibition Patrol to Warship**: Originally designed for anti-rum running during Prohibition, the vessel was repurposed for anti-submarine warfare and convoy escort duties .

4. **From Military to Commercial**: After decommissioning, the vessel was converted to various commercial roles including supply ship, geophysical exploration ship, and multi-purpose support vessel .

## 7. Conclusion

USCGC Dione (WPC-107) was a versatile patrol vessel that served the United States Coast Guard with distinction for nearly three decades . From her commissioning in 1934 through her decommissioning in 1963, Dione adapted to changing military and political circumstances, serving in both world wars and the early Cold War .

The vessel's service highlights the evolution of Coast Guard operations from peacetime law enforcement to wartime convoy escort and anti-submarine warfare . Her role as the sole patrol vessel during the early months of the U-boat campaign along the American East Coast underscores the challenges faced by the United States in defending its coastal waters during the early years of World War II .

Following her military service, Dione continued to serve in various commercial roles until at least 1992 . Her long service life and multiple adaptations demonstrate the durability and versatility of the Thetis/Argo-class design .

USCGC Dione represents an important piece of American naval and Coast Guard history, serving as a reminder of the vital role played by smaller vessels in both military and peacetime operations.

From her commissioning in 1934 through her decommissioning in 1963, Dione adapted to changing military and political circumstances.
Dione served in both world wars and the early Cold War.
The vessel's service highlights the evolution of Coast Guard operations from peacetime law enforcement to wartime convoy escort and anti-submarine warfare.

Her role as the sole patrol vessel during the early months of the U-boat campaign along the American East Coast underscores the challenges faced by the United States in defending its coastal waters during the early years of World War II.
Following her military service, Dione continued to serve in various commercial roles until at least 1992.
Her long service life and multiple adaptations demonstrate the durability and versatility of the Thetis/Argo-class design.
USCGC Dione represents an important piece of American naval and Coast Guard history.
USCGC Dione serves as a reminder of the vital role played by smaller vessels in both military and peacetime operations.

6.content:
Interview with James Eldon Wheeler [6/17/2015]

Sue Wheeler
Today's date is June the 17th, 2015. We are at [address redacted]. We'll be interviewing the veteran James Eldon Wheeler. The interviewer's name is Sue Wheeler. The court reporter is Courtney Whittington. Please state your name and address for the record.

James Eldon Wheeler
James Eldon Wheeler. [address redacted].

Sue Wheeler
Your place of birth?

James Eldon Wheeler
Red Oak, Iowa, on Knuckle Street in [birth date redacted]. And...

Sue Wheeler
What are the names of your parents?

James Eldon Wheeler
Clyde Wheeler and Harriet -- Harriet Frank Wheeler.

Sue Wheeler
Do you have any siblings?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes.

Sue Wheeler
How many and ages?

James Eldon Wheeler
Two, a brother and a sister. The brother is older; he's 84. The sister is younger, and she's 72.

Sue Wheeler
Where did you grow up?

James Eldon Wheeler
In several towns in Iowa and Nebraska.

Sue Wheeler
Were your parents in the military?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
Were your siblings in the military?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes. My brother was in the Army, and he went overseas to Japan.

Sue Wheeler
Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

James Eldon Wheeler
I enlisted.

Sue Wheeler
Where were you living at the time?

James Eldon Wheeler
At 2569 Pierce Street in Omaha, Nebraska.

Sue Wheeler
Why did you join?

James Eldon Wheeler
To keep from being drafted.

Sue Wheeler
Why did you pick the service branch you joined?

James Eldon Wheeler
We picked the Navy and they knew it wouldn't take Terry Fletcher, he was too big, too obese, so we opted to go to the Coast Guard instead.

Sue Wheeler
Do you recall your first days in the service?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes, ma'am.

Sue Wheeler
What did it feel like?

James Eldon Wheeler
It felt like you -- you'd left life to get in a prison.

Sue Wheeler
Tell me about your boot camp training experience.

James Eldon Wheeler
You're busy every day. They'd get you up with a bugle call, and you had to fall out in front of the barracks and have inspection before you did anything else. They checked your shave and your appearance and all that. I got sent back in to shave twice.

Sue Wheeler
Anything else about your training?

James Eldon Wheeler
It was pretty complete. You had different things on different days; and you'd have classroom instructions and field experiences, like when you went to the rifle range wouldn't be the same day that you went to the gym to work out. Everything was on a different day.

Sue Wheeler
What about the swimming training that you got for the Coast Guard?

James Eldon Wheeler
That was unique. You went in and you went up in the top of this building -- it was a Quonset hut -- and you got up in the top and then somebody would say, It's your turn, go ahead and jump in. Well, from the top of the Quonset hut, that water don't look that deep but it's 8 foot deep and 10 foot deep but from the top of the Quonset hut, it don't look like it's 6 inches deep. They say jump with your feet together and your legs crossed and it takes a while to get mentally ready to jump and then you go ahead and jump and you have to take off your pants in the water and come up and make a flotation device out of them. Tie the legs closed, throw them over your head, and catch air in them where you can get between the legs and float. And that's the main part I remember, you have to take your pants off and your shoes and socks and all that while you're in the water. That's not easy.

Sue Wheeler
Did you -- what about the training on the side where you had to stand there for a certain period of time?

James Eldon Wheeler
Oh, that was -- I can't remember his name. He was a turd; that's the best way to put it. He had no mercy on anybody. Stand at attention and if you fall, fold at attention and when you hit the water, it's a flat smack like you're getting hit in the face with a -- with a frying pan or something.

Sue Wheeler
Do you remember your instructors?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. I remember that was Push-Up Pete who was such a turd. He -- he would make them get down on the floor and give him ten or 20 push-ups. I'd liked to see him later. I don't think I could handle him right now.

Sue Wheeler
How did you get through it?

James Eldon Wheeler
You just got to grin and bear it, and keep your nasty thoughts to yourself because ain't nobody else listening.

Sue Wheeler
Were you awarded any medals or citations?

James Eldon Wheeler
I'm -- I'm thinking I got the sharpshooter medal; but that's one everybody, just about, gets.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. This will be about the experiences. Which war did you serve in?

James Eldon Wheeler
The Korean Conflict.

Sue Wheeler
Where exactly did you go?

James Eldon Wheeler
About as far as I went out of the United States was Havana, Cuba.

Sue Wheeler
Do you remember arriving in Havana?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes, ma'am. It -- it's as bad as Mexico. There's a drunk laying on the street, his mouth gapped open, his eyes shut and flies crawling in and out of his mouth and people walk up and walk by him and just step over him and keep on going, don't do anything. And that's very different from here in the United States. If you see somebody laying out on a sidewalk, you're going to find out what's wrong with him; but over there, they don't really care. That was a different experience altogether.

Sue Wheeler
How did that make you feel?

James Eldon Wheeler
I felt sorry for the people there; their conditions of living were terrible.

Sue Wheeler
What was your job and assignment?

James Eldon Wheeler
An assignment?

Sue Wheeler
Uh-huh, your job and your assignment.

James Eldon Wheeler
I was a Second Class Boatswain Mate, and mostly my job was maintaining the appearance of the ship, the painting, the polishing of the brass and making sure all the superstructure was clean and painted. After we went to Cuba, it turned all the -- all the paint on the ship gray and the Coast Guard ships are all painted white and we had a dingy gray ship.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. What -- was your job also -- did you see any combat?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. The only combat I saw was physical between other members of the service.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Didn't you have a job with -- having to do with shooting of the guns and...

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes, ma'am. I shot a 3-inch .50 caliber cannon and a 20 mm aircraft gun and a .30-06, just a regular -- regular rifle. Then I shot a .30-06 BAR, which is a combat rifle and when you shoot it, you lay down and get prone and it just drags you when you pull the trigger. You yell "charge" when you pull the trigger because it'll pull you right on down. They give that to the smallest man they can find because he makes a small target and that's the first guy that gets shot is the BAR because that rifle is an automatic and you can shoot multiple rounds very accurately.

Sue Wheeler
Were there any casualties in your unit?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. The only casualty -- or you'd call a casualty -- was a -- a cook that drank too much and he got sauced on a trip and they took him off the ship in a wraparound sport coat usually known as a straitjacket. We never did see him again.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Can you tell me about a couple of your most memorable experiences?

James Eldon Wheeler
Most memorable was -- was probably on the way to boot camp. We were on the train and we had just picked up some recruits in New York and I got an experience of the difference in the brogue that people use. In Texas, it's "y'all"; in New York and up there, there ain't no telling what it is. We were on a train and a guy said, Be careful, don't step on the Earl on the floor. I said, I don't see Earl. He said, It's right there. A big puddle of Earl. I said, That's oil. He said, That's what I said, Earl. Don't step on him; you'll slip and fall. That's my first experience with the brogue from the New York area.

Sue Wheeler
What about when y'all were out and you had to drink all the V8 juice?

James Eldon Wheeler
Oh, we set depth chargers to go off and it's supposed to be set at 60 feet and they set them at 6 feet and it blew the whole back end of the ship up out of the water and car- -- cracked the water tank and we lost our drinking water in the bilges and it was pumped out and we didn't have nothing to drink but V8 juice and I don't like V8 juice still yet. It's nasty. But when there ain't nothing else to drink, you drink it. Doesn't make any difference how nasty it tastes.

Sue Wheeler
What about your -- when you had to brush your teeth with the -- with the V8 juice also?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. You brush your teeth with V8 juice and rinsed your mouth out with V8 juice, and I still don't like V8 juice. I still don't drink it, don't touch it, don't want it in the house.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. We're going to speak about -- talk about your life while you were in the service. How did you stay in touch with your family?

James Eldon Wheeler
Mail.

Sue Wheeler
What was the food like?

James Eldon Wheeler
Some days it was good, other days it was terrible. It's like food that you eat every day at home only there's more of it; and if you get it on your plate, you're going to eat it. I got -- I thought -- was mashed potatoes one day and it was boiled squash and a scoop of mashed potatoes is a whole lot easier to eat than boiled squash that looked like potatoes.

Sue Wheeler
What'd you do with those squash?

James Eldon Wheeler
The first time, I ate them. The second time, I put them under the table. We got up and left them there and didn't get caught.

Sue Wheeler
Well, what about the cook that you were talking about that kind of went crazy frying the eggs?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah, he was -- he was different. You crack and throw it on top of the grill and if the ship's rolling, it'll run off the grill and hit the floor. He'd open probably six eggs and there was quite a mess on the floor at the end of the stove. He just didn't catch them when he broke them, and they run off the stove and hit the floor. You've got to catch them with a spatula when they run that way and put it in front of them where it'll hold it on top of the stove until it gets hot enough to cook, then it don't run off. But when you first bust them, that's so runny, it -- it flies off the stove.

Sue Wheeler
Did you have plenty of supplies?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah, you talk about food -- foodstuffs, normally we did. You have a different menu there. Every Sunday night you get cold cuts. Cold cuts is nobody's favorite meal; that's minced ham and the other type, liverwurst and all that. And those things have been on the ship for 14 days or more in a cooler, sometimes they'd get a little bit green looking; and you didn't like eating that. Sunday nights was not a real good night to eat on the ship. You had cold cuts and...

Sue Wheeler
Did you feel pressure or stress?

James Eldon Wheeler
Not often.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Was there something special that you did for good luck on there?

James Eldon Wheeler
You pray a lot, especially when it's rough weather. That ship don't go straight through the water; it rocks back and forth. And the ship said a 67-degree roll was critical; that's when they didn't come back up, they go on down. We took a 67-degree roll one night. We were coming around, heading to the passes after we left New Orleans; there was a hurricane out in the Gulf, and we tipped over 67 degrees. All the stuff off the lockers in the burling compartments fell to the floor or in the bed with you and it was sure hectic. I got up and grabbed the dogging wrench, which is a piece of pipe, maybe 12 or 14-inches long that you dog down the hatches with and took that in my hand and went up to the lifeboat station and the life raft that I was assigned to and the boys asked me, What's that dogging wrench for? I said, It's my ticket to the inside seat. Three people can sit inside and 18 are tied on around the outside; and I didn't want to be tied on the outside, my feet dangling for shark bait, so I got a ticket to the inside seat. I said, I will use that on anybody that tries to get my seat. Nobody volunteered to try to take my seat.

Sue Wheeler
How did the people entertain themselves? What was your entertainment on the ships?

James Eldon Wheeler
Movies and T- -- TV, mostly stories and whatever you can think of; but we had movies that we could trade with other ships -- we had John Wayne, and I can't remember the name of it now.

Sue Wheeler
Red River?

James Eldon Wheeler
Red River. And I saw that so many times I could just about tell you everything that was going to happen. I showed the movies on the back of the ship on the fantail up on a sheet, and we had that Red River for I don't know how many trips. I got plumb sick of that Red River. Everybody else did, too. We could tell you what the next -- next sneeze would be on there.

Sue Wheeler
What happened when you were going to try to exchange it with another ship?

James Eldon Wheeler
We had to go -- we were in Florida somewhere, it might have been at Santa Rosa Island, and there was an aircraft carrier there and we said, Go trade this Red River and get something that's good to watch. They said all right and they went in -- and there's a movie theater on the aircraft carrier, so they went down to the movie projection room and got a different movie, it said something on the outside of the case and damned if it didn't turn out to be Red River. We socked off Red River and got Red River. I never will forget that. I watched that way too many times.

Sue Wheeler
What did you do when you were on leave?

James Eldon Wheeler
I went home. Went around to check and see what all had changed in town and called my -- some of my friends to see what they were doing.

Sue Wheeler
Where did you travel while you were in service?

James Eldon Wheeler
Mostly to Havana, Cuba; and then we went to Baltimore and up towards New York and went to dry dock in Baltimore and they did some repairs. I went and played pool in -- in the officers' club -- non-commissioned officers' club, and I shot pool all night long. When I went to bed, I could still see pool balls rolling; and I decided I wouldn't do that again. I didn't get much sleep that night watching pool balls.

Sue Wheeler
Do you recall any particularly humorous or unusual event?

James Eldon Wheeler
Several.

Sue Wheeler
Want to elaborate a little bit?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. Joe Franks is a -- he's a Coonass from Louisiana, and the old boy -- I can't remember his name -- was from Dallas and they got into a conflict one night over who knows what. Joe Franks is about 5'6, 160 pounds and the other old boy was about 6'3, weighed about 220. And Joe Franks picked him up and threw him over the handrail off of the ship. You've got to be pretty scared to pick up a man that big and throw him over the handrail. Well, he come up out of the water, he climbed up the piling that was all full of barnacles and shells on it and he was blood from his nose to his toes and he come in -- in the lifeboat station saying, Where is that SOB? I'm going to kill him. I said, He ain't here. He's down on the ship. He said, I'll go down there and find him. I said, Go ahead; but you leave out of here. It was at night, must have been about 3:00 in the morning. As he come in the burling compartment, flipped on the lights -- and we got lights every 10 foot -- and he said, Didn't them lights blind you? I said, No. He come in, he had a meat cleaver in one hand and a big 'ole knife in the other one; and I was concentrating on the knife and the meat cleaver. And I told him the guy he was looking for wasn't there and he went back down to the ship and I went in and opened the small arms locker and got out a .45 and loaded it and called the ship and said don't let that sapsucker come back this way or I'm going to blow him back down the steps. He said, Well, we'll try and keep here. I said, You're going to keep him here or you can him kiss him goodbye because I'm going to kill him if he comes back up here. He said, All right. Settle down. And I settled down and we went on but that tickled me. It was a 60-watt lightbulb every 20 feet or so down that burling compartment on the lifeboat station; and that -- they had that court-martial -- the guy said, Didn't that light blind you when he first turned it on? I said, If you ever have the opportunity to wake up and there's light on where you can see and you see a guy with a meat cleaver and butcher knife standing right over your bunk and saying "Where is he? I'm going to kill him"; I said, Your eyes aren't fogged up, the light don't blind you. You see that knife and that cleaver, that's the main thing on your mind. And he got put in the high five for I don't know how long. His name was Grandstaff, and he got put in the brig.

Sue Wheeler
He didn't find that other guy?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. Well, the other guy went over the hill that night; and he went back to Dallas. He called in from Dallas saying, I know I'm gone; and I'm in trouble. He said, But I -- I wanted to call in and get my record straight of what -- said I was afraid he was going to kill me. He said, So the smartest thing I'd done was run home. That's 500 miles. He went back to Dallas to get away from that old boy, and he would -- would have killed him.

Sue Wheeler
Was that while y'all were still stationed out here at Freeport? Where were y'all stationed then?

James Eldon Wheeler
Freeport, Texas.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. And what about the night you were going to -- you were in charge of the -- the way you -- what did you do with Freddy? Oh, y'all were going out and...

James Eldon Wheeler
We were going out on liberty that night, and he got in trouble. I was on the Dione then, WPC-107. It's a 165-foot Coast Guard cutter; and they're built like a Canadian Corsair. They're long and slim and don't -- they aren't real stable going through the water. They -- they do good going over rough seas on up and down; but rocking sideways, they ain't very good. I can remember many a night bouncing in my bed. I had a wire -- a pipe-frame bed with a canvas mattress that you'd lace in on the bottom to give it a little cushion. Well, I'd put my foot out and my arms and legs out where I wouldn't fly out of bed; I'd just go up a little and fall back down. And if you didn't get in there good, you'd come out and you may bounce off four or five other bunks before you got down to ground level. There used to be a boatswain mate on there that his job was wake everybody up, and he was bad about grabbing them by the neck and just jerking them out and let them hit on the floor, said they woke up good that way. He said they often wanted to fight after they hit the floor, but they wasn't in no shape to really get it.

Sue Wheeler
I was talking about when you went to -- had to paint the deck. You were going to paint the deck.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah.

Sue Wheeler
That was punishment for your friend.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. Me and him -- I told him, We'll just stay and work overtime; and he -- of course he's mouthy; that's Freddy Mathis, an engineman. He got mouthy and I tipped a 5-gallon can of paint over his head that had a good skim in it where it wouldn't come out -- I didn't think -- and the skim broke and come down all over his head and got all over him. The first thing he done is hug me. All that paint on him got on me, and we've been friends ever since that.

Sue Wheeler
Anything else you remember about all that?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. I -- I can remember going on gunnery practice and I got congratulated for shooting down the plane -- or actually we shot targets that they pulled behind them and you shoot that 20 mm, it's like squirting a water hose. You've got tracers every fourth round and you just follow the red streak and get it where you want it to go and that's it. Of course, another funny thing that happened, we was on a training exercise and a guy -- the pilot of the plane pulling the -- the target said get -- get that crazy son of a bitch off of that cannon. He's aiming at me and that was Smitty, a gunner's mate, he'd come in sauced and he got on that plane and he was tracking him good. He'd pull the trigger and pull that plane out of sight.

Sue Wheeler
Did you keep a personal diary?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
All in your head, huh?

James Eldon Wheeler
All in the head and don't remember much of it anyway, just the highlights.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. I want to ask you a few questions about after your service. Do you recall the day your service ended?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes. I was at the Port of Galveston. I was getting discharged from Galveston and then had to take a train or something to get home, but I was in Galveston and was going to be discharged that evening and went to eat lunch. All the guys on the Galveston -- everybody get -- there was a bottle of milk. It was in the carton and they'd break open the carton, either quart-sized or pint-sized and then spit in it. And I said, Man, what are you doing? The other guy came up and said, I want some milk. And he said, Just a minute and you can have it. Spit in it again, handed him the milk; and that old boy laced him, knocked him flat as a flitter out there in the middle of the floor and said, No, you get up. And he spit in it and said, You drink it. And he drank it, but he didn't want no more of that fist. I don't know how much trouble he got into. I left out at lunchtime and headed for Nebraska.

Sue Wheeler
What did you do in the days and the weeks afterward?

James Eldon Wheeler
Nothing really stands out in my mind.

Sue Wheeler
Did you work, or did you go back to school?

James Eldon Wheeler
I worked. I went to work for Charles Snider Upholstery Company. That's where I worked before I went in the service.

Sue Wheeler
Was your -- did you get an education supported by the GI bill?

James Eldon Wheeler
I went and took two semesters at Omaha University. I was wanting to be a clinical psychologist; but that field is not easy to get into or to keep employed in, so I dropped out of college and went to work full-time.

Sue Wheeler
Did you make any close friendships while you were in the service?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes. Freddy David Mathis, a seaman; and we -- we've been in contact since '54. He's the only one that I -- well...

Sue Wheeler
Leroy.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah, that's not -- not true, so another one is Leroy Lender and then Bob O'Leary is another one. That's three. Is that 30 minutes?

Sue Wheeler
It says -- did you -- you continue those relationships?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes.

Sue Wheeler
Have you joined any veteran's organizations or anything?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Let's talk a little bit about your later years, and we'll close off after that. What did you go on to do as a career after the war after the -- your service?

James Eldon Wheeler
I was a carpenter for 28 years and working for Dow Chemical Company. And I worked as a carpenter, a carpenter apprentice, a carpenter foreman, a general -- general safety foreman for masons, insulators, riggers and carpenters and then I retired.

Sue Wheeler
Tell me a little bit about when you first started working for Dow, though. What was your beginning there?

James Eldon Wheeler
I worked in the yard department in -- patching holes in the drive -- driveways and entrances coming in. [Telephone ringing]

Sue Wheeler
About what you started -- when you started at Dow.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. I was in the concrete patching and road patching, picking up trash off the side of the road; and I went from that to being a carpenter apprentice. I was already working as a carpenter apprentice through the union program and then I was elected as an outstanding apprentice and took a trip to Chicago and came back and Dow put me as an apprentice and I worked through the apprentice program and come out and become a carpenter foreman. And as a carpenter foreman, I had a safety responsibility of the carpenters and then I had carpenters, masons and insulators and riggers to be -- to be in charge of their safety. Then I got promoted and went to Plant B, and I was over Plant B and Plant A masons and insulators and riggers and all that for both plants. I didn't like that.

Sue Wheeler
What about chlorine -- the chlorine plant?

James Eldon Wheeler
Oh, I was an area foreman for Chlorine 6, the biggest chlorine plant in the world. We made 5 million pounds of liquid chlorine every day and chlorine is -- it was used as a poison gas in World War I, and then they outlawed after that.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
How do you think your service and experiences there affected your life?

James Eldon Wheeler
Might have made me a little bit more easy to get along with.

Sue Wheeler
Is there anything you'd like to add that we haven't covered in this interview?

James Eldon Wheeler
Not really.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Well, I want to thank you for your service, thank you for giving us this interview; and we certainly appreciate your service to the country.

James Eldon Wheeler
You're welcome. (Interview concluded)

Years After World War II, Divers Explore Wreck Site of U-352
============================================================

When the German submarine U-352 was sunk during World War II, no one knew if its remains would ever be seen again. Today, divers visit the sub on almost daily excursions. But you don’t have to venture out to sea to get a glimpse of our state’s maritime history.

by [Todd Dulaney](https://www.ourstate.com/author/tdulaney/ "Posts by Todd Dulaney")

![Image 25: diver down](https://d3m7xw68ay40x8.cloudfront.net/assets/2015/05/18131028/diver-down.jpg)

Shipwreck divers are early risers. Dive charters head out around 6 a.m. so that customers have time to prep their equipment, run through their dive plan, tick off items on their safety checklist, double-check their safety checklist, and then actually get into the water and down to the wreck. One of the most sought-after wreck dives on the coast, though, isn’t even in the ocean. At the North Carolina Aquarium at Pine Knoll Shores, 60 volunteer divers from across the state — and another dozen members of the aquarium staff — vie to be a part of one of the two scheduled daily dives on a replica of one of the most famous wrecks in the Atlantic.

• • •
As Ethan Simmons goes over this afternoon’s dive plan, the three volunteer divers bobbing in the water check their gauges and breathing regulators. When Simmons, the aquarium’s dive safety officer, asks the divers if they are clear on that day’s tasks and if each knows what role he’ll play on the dive, each diver loudly says “yes.” A mere head nod won’t do.

Sure, diving on the aquarium’s three-quarter-size replica of the 220-foot-long German World War II submarine _U-352_ isn’t quite as daunting as a dive on the real thing — for one, the former is just 70 feet long and sits on the bottom of a 306,000-gallon aquarium tank in 15 feet of clear, well-lit, 77-degree salt water; the latter is on the bottom of the ocean in 115 feet of murky seawater that’s frigid in winter and like bathwater in summer. Still, safety and dive preparation are just as much a priority here as there.

Of course, divers can’t prepare for every circumstance. Today, unexpected forces cause the lead diver to deviate slightly from the plan Simmons laid out. Improvising, his fellow divers keep sharks at bay. The culprit? An itsy-bitsy spider. Or, more specifically, _the_ itsy-bitsy spider: On the spectator’s side of the tank’s eight-and-a-quarter-inch-thick acrylic window, a 4-year-old boy with his finger pressed against the window has engaged the diver in an impromptu duet of the kids’ song.

• • •
_U-352_ joined the list of an estimated 2,000 shipwrecks in North Carolina’s notorious Graveyard of the Atlantic more than 70 years ago, a period in the state’s nautical history that saw hundreds of vessels sent to the bottom of the ocean in the span of a matter of months. The sinkings began just weeks after the United States was pulled into World War II with the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor in the Pacific, when Nazi Germany brought the war to the North Carolina coast. Beginning with the January 19, 1942, torpedoing of the 337-foot-long U.S. freighter _City of Atlanta_ off the coast of Avon, German U-boats wreaked havoc on the shipping channel along the Outer Banks.

When the Nazi onslaught known as Operation _Paukenschlag_, or Operation Drumbeat, began, a single U.S. Coast Guard cutter, USCGC _Dione_, was responsible for protecting the entire East Coast — which might explain why German sub commanders referred to this period of the war as “American shooting season.” By July, almost 400 merchant ships had been sunk, earning the corridor the moniker Torpedo Alley.

By comparison, during that same period, only nine U-boats were sunk by U.S. forces — including four off the North Carolina coast.

In the midst of the Nazis’ 1942 incursion into American waters, the commander of the _U-352_ made the ill-fated decision on May 9, 1942, to attack the USCGC _Icarus_, which was on patrol for subs and ready to fight back. But when the sub’s torpedo exploded short of its target, the _Icarus_ responded with a depth-charge attack that forced the sub to the surface, where the crew then abandoned ship before the _U-352_ sank 28 nautical miles south of Morehead City. Thirty-three German sailors made it off the ship; 15 drowned on board.

The sub lay undisturbed until 1975, when the owner of the Olympus Dive Centert in Morehead City found the wreck. Today, the _U-352_ is one of the state’s top dive sites.

• • •
The aquarium’s re-created _U-352_ joined replicas of Blackbeard’s _Queen Anne’s Revenge_ and the World War II-era freighter _Caribsea_ in May 2006. The sub sits across the length of the 70-foot “Living Shipwreck” exhibit, listing toward spectators at a 45-degree angle. Its barnacle-encrusted conning tower — the raised area from where the Nazi skipper gave the orders to fire on unsuspecting Allied ships — creates a natural path for the swirl of fish, eels, and rays. For most people, the faux wreckage is as close as they’ll get to seeing the actual ship.

The scale version looks so much like the German warship that the aquarium display was used as a stand-in during a 2007 ceremony for survivors attended by Heinz Richter, one of the 33 Germans who made it off the sub. During the memorial, Simmons and Stuart May, the aquarium’s director of husbandry and operations, placed a wreath on the replica as a memorial for the sailors entombed on the actual _U-352_.

“A lot of people don’t think about it being a war grave,” Simmons says. Out of respect for those who perished, the aquarium doesn’t put decorations in the exhibit that might be inappropriate, like plastic skeletons at Halloween.

During the two daily interactive dives, though, when divers field questions from within the tank, few aquarium-goers ask about the sub’s war service, let alone the fate of its crew. People ask the divers how they got started. (May says he was inspired as a kid by the television show _Sea Hunt_; Simmons grew up near the North Carolina Aquarium at Fort Fisher and made his first dive in high school.) But the things most spectators, especially kids, want to know about have razor-sharp teeth and bad reputations: the sand tiger, sandbar, and nurse sharks that circle the divers in the tank.

_Do they ever eat the other fish? How do you keep from getting bitten? Are you afraid of the sharks?_ According to May: Yes, sharks eat other fish, but not often. Divers use sticks made from PVC pipes to encourage sharks to keep moving along. And no, he’s not afraid of the sharks in the tank.

“People watch too much TV,” May says.

• • •
Divers like May and Simmons — and the hundreds of others who venture under the waves — have man and Mother Nature to thank for the thousands of shipwrecks that litter the seafloor along North Carolina’s coast. Cannonballs have sunk wooden boats, torpedoes have brought down steel ships, and hurricanes have claimed everything from rickety sloops to mighty ironclads. Still more ships — as well as railroad boxcars and airplanes — have been sunk intentionally as part of the North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries’ artificial reef program. Once on the seafloor, time and tide beat, bury, and often recycle the helpless hulls.

For some ship captains, a quick trip down the coast on the swift current was worth the risk of crossing paths with a U-boat or hitting one of the Outer Banks’ treacherous sandbars, such as those at Diamond Shoals, Cape Lookout Shoals, and Frying Pan Shoals. And the costs and benefits remain — except for those pesky U-boats, of course.

“Sandbars didn’t go away,” says Benjamin Wunderly, the associate museum curator at the North Carolina Maritime Museums in Beaufort. “Charts and GPS help avoid sandbars, but it doesn’t mean hitting one can’t happen.”

The museum is filled with the stories behind the people and vessels involved in the shipwrecks. Many of the tales involve the three ships featured in the aquarium’s exhibits, like the wreck of the _Caribsea_, whose spar, Wunderly explains, was found on an Ocracoke beach and fashioned into a cross for the village’s Methodist church. And just as the aquarium provides a glimpse at what a few of the wrecks look like, the museum closes the gap in the narrative for these, and other, wrecks. To complete the experience, maritime history buffs could don masks and tanks and flippers, and see the wrecks on the sea floor for themselves, but Wunderly admits: “Man swimming around underwater just isn’t a natural thing to do” — especially in the Graveyard of the Atlantic.
