Recollections From Aviators
---------------------------

The Coast Guard Aviation Association began an Oral History Project during the annual Roost in 2016. These retired aviators gave their accounts of career experiences. Here are their stories.

###### My Life in the Coast Guard: A Conversation with CAPT David Oliver, Coast Guard Aviator #124

In September 1999 Tom Stanback sat down with CAPT David Oliver, USCG (retired) in his hometown of Wilmington, NC to discuss his career (1941-1970). The outcome of this interview was a booklet titled “My Life in the Coast Guard”.

CAPT Oliver had an interesting and diverse career from serving aboard USCGC DIONE performing coastal convoy escort duty early in WWII to earning his wings and flying anti-submarine patrols and coastal search and rescue late in WWII. He was an early convert to helicopters at Air Station Brooklyn (December 1944) and flew several important rescues at the Rotary Wing Development Unit during a pivotal time when the Coast Guard was struggling with acceptance of the helicopter as a rescue asset. In addition, he flew International Ice Patrol missions and was the CO of the first Helicopter Port Security Detachment during the Korean War. He later served at Air Detachment Kodiak, AK; Air Station San Francisco, CA; and Air Station New Orleans, LA.

###### Speaker: Lt. Art Ross, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I wish to recount a rather small episode when I was attached to Air Station Borinquen in Puerto Rico. We were flying normally search and rescue. thoruought the Carribean. But I was tasked one time to carry the Admiral on a rather awkward mission throughout the islands…”

###### Speaker: Capt. Bob Workman, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I’m Bob Workman. I’m a retired Coast Guard Captain. Coast Guard aviator number is 914, and Coast Guard helicopter pilot number 458. My wife says I belong in a museum…”

###### Speaker: CMR. Bruce Melnick

Audio Player

“I retired as a commander from the Coast Guard as an aviator and Coast Guard Astronaut number one, in 1992. I think I had one of the most amazing careers and I feel like I’m one of the luckiest people on this planet…”

###### Speaker: AD1 Carl Saylor, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I enlisted back in the Coast Guard in July of 1977. At the time, I really didn’t have any other options. My dad kind of pointed me in that direction. I always wanted to be a helicopter crew member. Loved the thought of flying…”

###### Speaker: Lt. CMR Dave Cooper, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I began my Coast Guard career at OCS in Yorktown in 1968. After graduating there and being commissioned as an ensign by my father, who was a retired marine colonel, I went to New Castle, New Hampshire and reported aboard the U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Active (WMEC-618), a 210…”

###### Speaker: Capt. Dave Spillman, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I went to the Coast Guard Academy. Graduated in 1979, then I went to the Coast Guard Cutter Dependable in Panama City, Florida, for about a year, and then I went to flight school. I graduated from there in I think it was October of 1981. Transitioned to the H-52…”

###### Speaker: Lt. CMR Dennis Turner, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I was a direct commission aviator, so I actually started in the Navy in 1971. I was actually stationed in Guantanamo where they had the last Navy HU-16’s, and then transitioned to C-131’s…”

###### Speaker: CMR Don Winchester, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I’m a 1966 graduate of the Academy. I spent a year on the ship Matagorda, a sea plane tender, ocean station vessel out of Honolulu, Hawaii. A year in flight training, ’67-’68. My first air station was San Francisco….”

###### Speaker: CMR Frank L. Shelley, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“Coast Guard Academy Class of 1949, and Coast Guard Aviator number 633. Okay, I … initially graduated from the Coast Guard, graduation with the Coast Guard Academy … I lucked out and went to a buoy tender in Monterey, California. And it was so good it couldn’t possibly last, and it didn’t…”

###### Speaker: Vice Admiral Howie Thorsen, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

” I graduated from the Coast Guard Academy in 1955. We spent two years at sea in Coast Guard Cutter Ingham, usually in the north Atlantic, and weather patrol, refresher training, that type of thing, and then fortunately got orders to flight training…”

###### Speaker: Capt. Jeff Pettitt, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I flew for 28 years of my 30 years in the Coast Guard. That was a charmed time to be flying. I got my wings in 81 and retired in 2009. While a lot of these guys have some incredible stories to tell, I like to tell a lighter side of things…”

###### Speaker: CMR John Lewis, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

” A long time ago, it seems that I may have made the last official water landing in the Coast Guard A216 Echo, the Albatross. More affectionately known as the Goat…”

###### Speaker: Capt. Les High, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

” Only been retired for 41 years. I started in the Coast Guard back in the ’40s during the war, and I was going to college for a couple of years. While I was there, my dad told me about the opportunity with the Coast Guard Academy, and I went to the Coast Guard Academy…”

###### Speaker: Mario Marini, USCG

Audio Player

” I joined the Coast Guard in August of 1980. I went to my aviation school at Elizabeth City, North Carolina, in 1985, when the rescue swimmer program was just starting out for the Coast Guard. I was assigned to Air Station Kodiak in January of 1986…”

###### Speaker: Capt. Merrill Wood, USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I think I may have been a second senior captain in the Coast Guard when I retired in November 30th of 1984, yes. Now we’re going to talk about where we went and how we got there…”

###### Speaker: Senior Chief AE Capt. Tom Wynn USCG (Ret.)

Audio Player

“I joined when I was 17 years old in 1972, July the 27th at noon. I remember that because there was a picture of me when the clock is in the picture of me swearing in. I swore in here in Mobile. I went to Davidson High School here…”

5.title: James Eldon Wheeler Collection
5.description: Boatswain's Mate Second Class, Coast Guard, Cold War - Cuba; Atlantic Ocean; New York; Baltimore, Maryland.
5.content:
Interview with James Eldon Wheeler [6/17/2015]

Sue Wheeler
Today's date is June the 17th, 2015. We are at [address redacted]. We'll be interviewing the veteran James Eldon Wheeler. The interviewer's name is Sue Wheeler. The court reporter is Courtney Whittington. Please state your name and address for the record.

James Eldon Wheeler
James Eldon Wheeler. [address redacted].

Sue Wheeler
Your place of birth?

James Eldon Wheeler
Red Oak, Iowa, on Knuckle Street in [birth date redacted]. And...

Sue Wheeler
What are the names of your parents?

James Eldon Wheeler
Clyde Wheeler and Harriet -- Harriet Frank Wheeler.

Sue Wheeler
Do you have any siblings?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes.

Sue Wheeler
How many and ages?

James Eldon Wheeler
Two, a brother and a sister. The brother is older; he's 84. The sister is younger, and she's 72.

Sue Wheeler
Where did you grow up?

James Eldon Wheeler
In several towns in Iowa and Nebraska.

Sue Wheeler
Were your parents in the military?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
Were your siblings in the military?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes. My brother was in the Army, and he went overseas to Japan.

Sue Wheeler
Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

James Eldon Wheeler
I enlisted.

Sue Wheeler
Where were you living at the time?

James Eldon Wheeler
At 2569 Pierce Street in Omaha, Nebraska.

Sue Wheeler
Why did you join?

James Eldon Wheeler
To keep from being drafted.

Sue Wheeler
Why did you pick the service branch you joined?

James Eldon Wheeler
We picked the Navy and they knew it wouldn't take Terry Fletcher, he was too big, too obese, so we opted to go to the Coast Guard instead.

Sue Wheeler
Do you recall your first days in the service?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes, ma'am.

Sue Wheeler
What did it feel like?

James Eldon Wheeler
It felt like you -- you'd left life to get in a prison.

Sue Wheeler
Tell me about your boot camp training experience.

James Eldon Wheeler
You're busy every day. They'd get you up with a bugle call, and you had to fall out in front of the barracks and have inspection before you did anything else. They checked your shave and your appearance and all that. I got sent back in to shave twice.

Sue Wheeler
Anything else about your training?

James Eldon Wheeler
It was pretty complete. You had different things on different days; and you'd have classroom instructions and field experiences, like when you went to the rifle range wouldn't be the same day that you went to the gym to work out. Everything was on a different day.

Sue Wheeler
What about the swimming training that you got for the Coast Guard?

James Eldon Wheeler
That was unique. You went in and you went up in the top of this building -- it was a Quonset hut -- and you got up in the top and then somebody would say, It's your turn, go ahead and jump in. Well, from the top of the Quonset hut, that water don't look that deep but it's 8 foot deep and 10 foot deep but from the top of the Quonset hut, it don't look like it's 6 inches deep. They say jump with your feet together and your legs crossed and it takes a while to get mentally ready to jump and then you go ahead and jump and you have to take off your pants in the water and come up and make a flotation device out of them. Tie the legs closed, throw them over your head, and catch air in them where you can get between the legs and float. And that's the main part I remember, you have to take your pants off and your shoes and socks and all that while you're in the water. That's not easy.

Sue Wheeler
Did you -- what about the training on the side where you had to stand there for a certain period of time?

James Eldon Wheeler
Oh, that was -- I can't remember his name. He was a turd; that's the best way to put it. He had no mercy on anybody. Stand at attention and if you fall, fold at attention and when you hit the water, it's a flat smack like you're getting hit in the face with a -- with a frying pan or something.

Sue Wheeler
Do you remember your instructors?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. I remember that was Push-Up Pete who was such a turd. He -- he would make them get down on the floor and give him ten or 20 push-ups. I'd liked to see him later. I don't think I could handle him right now.

Sue Wheeler
How did you get through it?

James Eldon Wheeler
You just got to grin and bear it, and keep your nasty thoughts to yourself because ain't nobody else listening.

Sue Wheeler
Were you awarded any medals or citations?

James Eldon Wheeler
I'm -- I'm thinking I got the sharpshooter medal; but that's one everybody, just about, gets.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. This will be about the experiences. Which war did you serve in?

James Eldon Wheeler
The Korean Conflict.

Sue Wheeler
Where exactly did you go?

James Eldon Wheeler
About as far as I went out of the United States was Havana, Cuba.

Sue Wheeler
Do you remember arriving in Havana?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes, ma'am. It -- it's as bad as Mexico. There's a drunk laying on the street, his mouth gapped open, his eyes shut and flies crawling in and out of his mouth and people walk up and walk by him and just step over him and keep on going, don't do anything. And that's very different from here in the United States. If you see somebody laying out on a sidewalk, you're going to find out what's wrong with him; but over there, they don't really care. That was a different experience altogether.

Sue Wheeler
How did that make you feel?

James Eldon Wheeler
I felt sorry for the people there; their conditions of living were terrible.

Sue Wheeler
What was your job and assignment?

James Eldon Wheeler
An assignment?

Sue Wheeler
Uh-huh, your job and your assignment.

James Eldon Wheeler
I was a Second Class Boatswain Mate, and mostly my job was maintaining the appearance of the ship, the painting, the polishing of the brass and making sure all the superstructure was clean and painted. After we went to Cuba, it turned all the -- all the paint on the ship gray and the Coast Guard ships are all painted white and we had a dingy gray ship.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. What -- was your job also -- did you see any combat?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. The only combat I saw was physical between other members of the service.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Didn't you have a job with -- having to do with shooting of the guns and...

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes, ma'am. I shot a 3-inch .50 caliber cannon and a 20 mm aircraft gun and a .30-06, just a regular -- regular rifle. Then I shot a .30-06 BAR, which is a combat rifle and when you shoot it, you lay down and get prone and it just drags you when you pull the trigger. You yell "charge" when you pull the trigger because it'll pull you right on down. They give that to the smallest man they can find because he makes a small target and that's the first guy that gets shot is the BAR because that rifle is an automatic and you can shoot multiple rounds very accurately.

Sue Wheeler
Were there any casualties in your unit?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. The only casualty -- or you'd call a casualty -- was a -- a cook that drank too much and he got sauced on a trip and they took him off the ship in a wraparound sport coat usually known as a straitjacket. We never did see him again.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Can you tell me about a couple of your most memorable experiences?

James Eldon Wheeler
Most memorable was -- was probably on the way to boot camp. We were on the train and we had just picked up some recruits in New York and I got an experience of the difference in the brogue that people use. In Texas, it's "y'all"; in New York and up there, there ain't no telling what it is. We were on a train and a guy said, Be careful, don't step on the Earl on the floor. I said, I don't see Earl. He said, It's right there. A big puddle of Earl. I said, That's oil. He said, That's what I said, Earl. Don't step on him; you'll slip and fall. That's my first experience with the brogue from the New York area.

Sue Wheeler
What about when y'all were out and you had to drink all the V8 juice?

James Eldon Wheeler
Oh, we set depth chargers to go off and it's supposed to be set at 60 feet and they set them at 6 feet and it blew the whole back end of the ship up out of the water and car- -- cracked the water tank and we lost our drinking water in the bilges and it was pumped out and we didn't have nothing to drink but V8 juice and I don't like V8 juice still yet. It's nasty. But when there ain't nothing else to drink, you drink it. Doesn't make any difference how nasty it tastes.

Sue Wheeler
What about your -- when you had to brush your teeth with the -- with the V8 juice also?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. You brush your teeth with V8 juice and rinsed your mouth out with V8 juice, and I still don't like V8 juice. I still don't drink it, don't touch it, don't want it in the house.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. We're going to speak about -- talk about your life while you were in the service. How did you stay in touch with your family?

James Eldon Wheeler
Mail.

Sue Wheeler
What was the food like?

James Eldon Wheeler
Some days it was good, other days it was terrible. It's like food that you eat every day at home only there's more of it; and if you get it on your plate, you're going to eat it. I got -- I thought -- was mashed potatoes one day and it was boiled squash and a scoop of mashed potatoes is a whole lot easier to eat than boiled squash that looked like potatoes.

Sue Wheeler
What'd you do with those squash?

James Eldon Wheeler
The first time, I ate them. The second time, I put them under the table. We got up and left them there and didn't get caught.

Sue Wheeler
Well, what about the cook that you were talking about that kind of went crazy frying the eggs?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah, he was -- he was different. You crack and throw it on top of the grill and if the ship's rolling, it'll run off the grill and hit the floor. He'd open probably six eggs and there was quite a mess on the floor at the end of the stove. He just didn't catch them when he broke them, and they run off the stove and hit the floor. You've got to catch them with a spatula when they run that way and put it in front of them where it'll hold it on top of the stove until it gets hot enough to cook, then it don't run off. But when you first bust them, that's so runny, it -- it flies off the stove.

Sue Wheeler
Did you have plenty of supplies?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah, you talk about food -- foodstuffs, normally we did. You have a different menu there. Every Sunday night you get cold cuts. Cold cuts is nobody's favorite meal; that's minced ham and the other type, liverwurst and all that. And those things have been on the ship for 14 days or more in a cooler, sometimes they'd get a little bit green looking; and you didn't like eating that. Sunday nights was not a real good night to eat on the ship. You had cold cuts and...

Sue Wheeler
Did you feel pressure or stress?

James Eldon Wheeler
Not often.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Was there something special that you did for good luck on there?

James Eldon Wheeler
You pray a lot, especially when it's rough weather. That ship don't go straight through the water; it rocks back and forth. And the ship said a 67-degree roll was critical; that's when they didn't come back up, they go on down. We took a 67-degree roll one night. We were coming around, heading to the passes after we left New Orleans; there was a hurricane out in the Gulf, and we tipped over 67 degrees. All the stuff off the lockers in the burling compartments fell to the floor or in the bed with you and it was sure hectic. I got up and grabbed the dogging wrench, which is a piece of pipe, maybe 12 or 14-inches long that you dog down the hatches with and took that in my hand and went up to the lifeboat station and the life raft that I was assigned to and the boys asked me, What's that dogging wrench for? I said, It's my ticket to the inside seat. Three people can sit inside and 18 are tied on around the outside; and I didn't want to be tied on the outside, my feet dangling for shark bait, so I got a ticket to the inside seat. I said, I will use that on anybody that tries to get my seat. Nobody volunteered to try to take my seat.

Sue Wheeler
How did the people entertain themselves? What was your entertainment on the ships?

James Eldon Wheeler
Movies and T- -- TV, mostly stories and whatever you can think of; but we had movies that we could trade with other ships -- we had John Wayne, and I can't remember the name of it now.

Sue Wheeler
Red River?

James Eldon Wheeler
Red River. And I saw that so many times I could just about tell you everything that was going to happen. I showed the movies on the back of the ship on the fantail up on a sheet, and we had that Red River for I don't know how many trips. I got plumb sick of that Red River. Everybody else did, too. We could tell you what the next -- next sneeze would be on there.

Sue Wheeler
What happened when you were going to try to exchange it with another ship?

James Eldon Wheeler
We had to go -- we were in Florida somewhere, it might have been at Santa Rosa Island, and there was an aircraft carrier there and we said, Go trade this Red River and get something that's good to watch. They said all right and they went in -- and there's a movie theater on the aircraft carrier, so they went down to the movie projection room and got a different movie, it said something on the outside of the case and damned if it didn't turn out to be Red River. We socked off Red River and got Red River. I never will forget that. I watched that way too many times.

Sue Wheeler
What did you do when you were on leave?

James Eldon Wheeler
I went home. Went around to check and see what all had changed in town and called my -- some of my friends to see what they were doing.

Sue Wheeler
Where did you travel while you were in service?

James Eldon Wheeler
Mostly to Havana, Cuba; and then we went to Baltimore and up towards New York and went to dry dock in Baltimore and they did some repairs. I went and played pool in -- in the officers' club -- non-commissioned officers' club, and I shot pool all night long. When I went to bed, I could still see pool balls rolling; and I decided I wouldn't do that again. I didn't get much sleep that night watching pool balls.

Sue Wheeler
Do you recall any particularly humorous or unusual event?

James Eldon Wheeler
Several.

Sue Wheeler
Want to elaborate a little bit?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. Joe Franks is a -- he's a Coonass from Louisiana, and the old boy -- I can't remember his name -- was from Dallas and they got into a conflict one night over who knows what. Joe Franks is about 5'6, 160 pounds and the other old boy was about 6'3, weighed about 220. And Joe Franks picked him up and threw him over the handrail off of the ship. You've got to be pretty scared to pick up a man that big and throw him over the handrail. Well, he come up out of the water, he climbed up the piling that was all full of barnacles and shells on it and he was blood from his nose to his toes and he come in -- in the lifeboat station saying, Where is that SOB? I'm going to kill him. I said, He ain't here. He's down on the ship. He said, I'll go down there and find him. I said, Go ahead; but you leave out of here. It was at night, must have been about 3:00 in the morning. As he come in the burling compartment, flipped on the lights -- and we got lights every 10 foot -- and he said, Didn't them lights blind you? I said, No. He come in, he had a meat cleaver in one hand and a big 'ole knife in the other one; and I was concentrating on the knife and the meat cleaver. And I told him the guy he was looking for wasn't there and he went back down to the ship and I went in and opened the small arms locker and got out a .45 and loaded it and called the ship and said don't let that sapsucker come back this way or I'm going to blow him back down the steps. He said, Well, we'll try and keep here. I said, You're going to keep him here or you can him kiss him goodbye because I'm going to kill him if he comes back up here. He said, All right. Settle down. And I settled down and we went on but that tickled me. It was a 60-watt lightbulb every 20 feet or so down that burling compartment on the lifeboat station; and that -- they had that court-martial -- the guy said, Didn't that light blind you when he first turned it on? I said, If you ever have the opportunity to wake up and there's light on where you can see and you see a guy with a meat cleaver and butcher knife standing right over your bunk and saying "Where is he? I'm going to kill him"; I said, Your eyes aren't fogged up, the light don't blind you. You see that knife and that cleaver, that's the main thing on your mind. And he got put in the high five for I don't know how long. His name was Grandstaff, and he got put in the brig.

Sue Wheeler
He didn't find that other guy?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. Well, the other guy went over the hill that night; and he went back to Dallas. He called in from Dallas saying, I know I'm gone; and I'm in trouble. He said, But I -- I wanted to call in and get my record straight of what -- said I was afraid he was going to kill me. He said, So the smartest thing I'd done was run home. That's 500 miles. He went back to Dallas to get away from that old boy, and he would -- would have killed him.

Sue Wheeler
Was that while y'all were still stationed out here at Freeport? Where were y'all stationed then?

James Eldon Wheeler
Freeport, Texas.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. And what about the night you were going to -- you were in charge of the -- the way you -- what did you do with Freddy? Oh, y'all were going out and...

James Eldon Wheeler
We were going out on liberty that night, and he got in trouble. I was on the Dione then, WPC-107. It's a 165-foot Coast Guard cutter; and they're built like a Canadian Corsair. They're long and slim and don't -- they aren't real stable going through the water. They -- they do good going over rough seas on up and down; but rocking sideways, they ain't very good. I can remember many a night bouncing in my bed. I had a wire -- a pipe-frame bed with a canvas mattress that you'd lace in on the bottom to give it a little cushion. Well, I'd put my foot out and my arms and legs out where I wouldn't fly out of bed; I'd just go up a little and fall back down. And if you didn't get in there good, you'd come out and you may bounce off four or five other bunks before you got down to ground level. There used to be a boatswain mate on there that his job was wake everybody up, and he was bad about grabbing them by the neck and just jerking them out and let them hit on the floor, said they woke up good that way. He said they often wanted to fight after they hit the floor, but they wasn't in no shape to really get it.

Sue Wheeler
I was talking about when you went to -- had to paint the deck. You were going to paint the deck.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah.

Sue Wheeler
That was punishment for your friend.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. Me and him -- I told him, We'll just stay and work overtime; and he -- of course he's mouthy; that's Freddy Mathis, an engineman. He got mouthy and I tipped a 5-gallon can of paint over his head that had a good skim in it where it wouldn't come out -- I didn't think -- and the skim broke and come down all over his head and got all over him. The first thing he done is hug me. All that paint on him got on me, and we've been friends ever since that.

Sue Wheeler
Anything else you remember about all that?

James Eldon Wheeler
No. I -- I can remember going on gunnery practice and I got congratulated for shooting down the plane -- or actually we shot targets that they pulled behind them and you shoot that 20 mm, it's like squirting a water hose. You've got tracers every fourth round and you just follow the red streak and get it where you want it to go and that's it. Of course, another funny thing that happened, we was on a training exercise and a guy -- the pilot of the plane pulling the -- the target said get -- get that crazy son of a bitch off of that cannon. He's aiming at me and that was Smitty, a gunner's mate, he'd come in sauced and he got on that plane and he was tracking him good. He'd pull the trigger and pull that plane out of sight.

Sue Wheeler
Did you keep a personal diary?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
All in your head, huh?

James Eldon Wheeler
All in the head and don't remember much of it anyway, just the highlights.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. I want to ask you a few questions about after your service. Do you recall the day your service ended?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes. I was at the Port of Galveston. I was getting discharged from Galveston and then had to take a train or something to get home, but I was in Galveston and was going to be discharged that evening and went to eat lunch. All the guys on the Galveston -- everybody get -- there was a bottle of milk. It was in the carton and they'd break open the carton, either quart-sized or pint-sized and then spit in it. And I said, Man, what are you doing? The other guy came up and said, I want some milk. And he said, Just a minute and you can have it. Spit in it again, handed him the milk; and that old boy laced him, knocked him flat as a flitter out there in the middle of the floor and said, No, you get up. And he spit in it and said, You drink it. And he drank it, but he didn't want no more of that fist. I don't know how much trouble he got into. I left out at lunchtime and headed for Nebraska.

Sue Wheeler
What did you do in the days and the weeks afterward?

James Eldon Wheeler
Nothing really stands out in my mind.

Sue Wheeler
Did you work, or did you go back to school?

James Eldon Wheeler
I worked. I went to work for Charles Snider Upholstery Company. That's where I worked before I went in the service.

Sue Wheeler
Was your -- did you get an education supported by the GI bill?

James Eldon Wheeler
I went and took two semesters at Omaha University. I was wanting to be a clinical psychologist; but that field is not easy to get into or to keep employed in, so I dropped out of college and went to work full-time.

Sue Wheeler
Did you make any close friendships while you were in the service?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes. Freddy David Mathis, a seaman; and we -- we've been in contact since '54. He's the only one that I -- well...

Sue Wheeler
Leroy.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah, that's not -- not true, so another one is Leroy Lender and then Bob O'Leary is another one. That's three. Is that 30 minutes?

Sue Wheeler
It says -- did you -- you continue those relationships?

James Eldon Wheeler
Yes.

Sue Wheeler
Have you joined any veteran's organizations or anything?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Let's talk a little bit about your later years, and we'll close off after that. What did you go on to do as a career after the war after the -- your service?

James Eldon Wheeler
I was a carpenter for 28 years and working for Dow Chemical Company. And I worked as a carpenter, a carpenter apprentice, a carpenter foreman, a general -- general safety foreman for masons, insulators, riggers and carpenters and then I retired.

Sue Wheeler
Tell me a little bit about when you first started working for Dow, though. What was your beginning there?

James Eldon Wheeler
I worked in the yard department in -- patching holes in the drive -- driveways and entrances coming in. [Telephone ringing]

Sue Wheeler
About what you started -- when you started at Dow.

James Eldon Wheeler
Yeah. I was in the concrete patching and road patching, picking up trash off the side of the road; and I went from that to being a carpenter apprentice. I was already working as a carpenter apprentice through the union program and then I was elected as an outstanding apprentice and took a trip to Chicago and came back and Dow put me as an apprentice and I worked through the apprentice program and come out and become a carpenter foreman. And as a carpenter foreman, I had a safety responsibility of the carpenters and then I had carpenters, masons and insulators and riggers to be -- to be in charge of their safety. Then I got promoted and went to Plant B, and I was over Plant B and Plant A masons and insulators and riggers and all that for both plants. I didn't like that.

Sue Wheeler
What about chlorine -- the chlorine plant?

James Eldon Wheeler
Oh, I was an area foreman for Chlorine 6, the biggest chlorine plant in the world. We made 5 million pounds of liquid chlorine every day and chlorine is -- it was used as a poison gas in World War I, and then they outlawed after that.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

James Eldon Wheeler
No.

Sue Wheeler
How do you think your service and experiences there affected your life?

James Eldon Wheeler
Might have made me a little bit more easy to get along with.

Sue Wheeler
Is there anything you'd like to add that we haven't covered in this interview?

James Eldon Wheeler
Not really.

Sue Wheeler
Okay. Well, I want to thank you for your service, thank you for giving us this interview; and we certainly appreciate your service to the country.

James Eldon Wheeler
You're welcome. (Interview concluded)

The [Battle of the Atlantic](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/world-war-ii/battle-of-the-atlantic.html) was the longest engagement of the Second World War, with the _Kriegsmarine_ reigning supreme in the ocean for much of the early stages. In December 1941, _Konteradmiral_ Karl Dönitz, commander of the U-boat fleet, launched an operation that caused devastation to Allied vessels in the first half of the following year, with almost 400 ships lost in one area in particular: Torpedo Junction.

Operation _Paukenschlag_
------------------------

 ![Image 1: Portrait of Karl Dönitz](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/64/2024/07/karl-donitz-1943-57641-470x640.jpg)

Karl Dönitz, 1943. (Photo Credit: ullstein bild / Getty Images)

The [Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/world-war-ii/james-r-ward-pearl-harbor.html) on December 7, 1941, thrust the United States into [World War II](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/world-war-ii/mickey-rooney.html). With the nation no longer neutral, the Germans were ready to strike, with [Karl Dönitz](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/world-war-ii/karl-donitz-cmdr-kriegsmarine.html) quickly putting together and implementing a plan-of-action to attack America’s poorly-guarded Atlantic coast.

Codenamed [Operation _Paukenschlag_](https://codenames.info/operation/paukenschlag/), the plan was the leverage the [_Kriegsmarine_](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/world-war-ii/operation-wikinger.html)‘s experience in the Atlantic to take out vessels navigating the busy shipping lanes off the coast of North Carolina’s Outer Banks – particularly, Capes Lookout and Hatteras.

Ill-prepared for attacks along the East Coast
---------------------------------------------

 ![Image 2: SS Dixie Arrow shrouded in smoke at sea](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/64/2024/07/torpedo-junction-allied-tanker-13283-741x536.jpg)

German U-boat _U-71_ sinking the SS _Dixie Arrow_ off Cape Hatteras, 1942. (Photo Credit: U.S. Navy / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain)

Even without previous experience, the U-boat crews navigating the East Coast of the United States would have been able to inflict devastation upon the vessels transiting through what became known as Torpedo Junction (or Torpedo Alley). For starters, vessels using the shipping lanes had grown complacent in the interwar years, ditching the defensive [zig-zag travel patterns](https://www.rmg.co.uk/stories/blog/curatorial/zig-zagging-how-confuse-enemy-sea) that had been developed to lessen the threat of enemy torpedoes.

While one might think that wouldn’t have been a big deal, given the US Navy’s presence, think again. Just a single ship patrolled the entire region, the USCGC _Dione_ (WPC-107); other ships had been stationed elsewhere, not that they were equipped for anti-submarine patrols, should they have been moved to the area.

Then there were issues on-shore. No blackouts were implemented, meaning any vessel sailing off the coast had a bright backdrop that made it easy to spot. There were also no patrol aircraft in the region, as they’d been assigned elsewhere, and help offered by the British Royal Navy was rejected, despite the American ally having personally experienced the wrath of the _Kriegsmarine_‘s U-boat fleet.

Notable incidents in Torpedo Junction
-------------------------------------

 ![Image 3: US Navy sailors and civilians watching as more sailors carry a coffin on a dark night](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/64/2024/07/u-85-sinking-funeral-98723-741x589.jpg)

Funeral for the casualties of the sinking of _U-85_, at Hampton National Cemetery, Virginia, 1942. (Photo Credit: USN / Naval History and Heritage Command / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain)

From January to June 1942, the _Kriegsmarine_ sunk 397 Allied vessels in Torpedo Junction – a staggering number for such a short period of time, especially against a major superpower like the United States. In comparison, the American forces were only able to sink three U-boats during this timeframe.

Of the 400 overall incidents that occurred, two stand out. The [first](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torpedo_Alley#Allied_vessels) was the losses of the SS _Empire Gem_ and _Venore_ in the early hours of January 24. The two Allied merchant vessels were unescorted, providing the Type _IXC_ U-boat _U-66_ the opportunity to attack. The enemy vessel fired several torpedoes, taking out both ships. Of their combined crews, 72 perished, while another 23 were rescued.

The [second notable event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torpedo_Alley#German_U-boats) involved the sinking of a German vessel. On April 13, 1942, the Type _VIIB_ U-boat _U-85_ took on the US Navy destroyer USS _Roper_ (DD-147). A firefight ensued between the two, with the latter securing a hit, before dropping 11 depth charges into the water. The enemy submarine sank, killing everyone onboard.

Criticizing the US Navy
-----------------------

 ![Image 4: Military portrait of Ernest J. King](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/64/2024/07/ernest-j-king-portrait-63966-441x640.jpg)

Ernest J. King, 1945. (Photo Credit: Keystone / Getty Images)

As the number of losses began to add up in Torpedo Junction, so, too, did criticism of the US Navy. This was lost on Adm. Ernest King, commander-in-chief of the US Fleet, who failed to understand why defending the Eastern Seaboard was so important. Any patrol aircraft that came available continued to be sent elsewhere, as did destroyers, and repeated offers from the British to help continued to be turned down.

On top of this, [efforts were made](https://ussnautilus.org/torpedo-junction/) to keep what was happening in the Atlantic out of the media, to ensure the public didn’t panic.

One of the few military officials to recognize the importance of diverting resources to Torpedo Junction was Brig. Gen. George C. Marshall, who, at the time, was the US Army’s chief of staff. He’s [quoted as saying](https://www.nps.gov/articles/wwii_caha_torpedo_junction.htm):

“The losses by submarines off our Atlantic seaboard and in the Caribbean now threaten our entire war effort… I am fearful that another month or two of this will so cripple our means of transport that we will be unable to bring sufficient men and planes to bear against the enemy in critical theaters to exercise a determining influence on the war.”

Fighting back against the Germans in Torpedo Junction
-----------------------------------------------------

 ![Image 5: SS Byron D. Benson shrouded in smoke at sea](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/64/2024/07/torpedo-alley-ss-benson-52802-741x599.jpg)

SS _Byron D. Benson_ torpedoed off Southern Shores, North Carolina, 1942. (Photo Credit: Unknown Author / National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration / Wikimedia Commons / Public Domain)

As the middle of 1942 neared, attacks in Torpedo Junction were [so frequent](https://coastalreview.org/2022/07/u-boat-artifacts-divers-reveal-history-of-torpedo-junction/) that the flaming vessels “burned so brightly \[…\] that on shore, it was said, one could read a newspaper by the glow at night, while the grim flotsam of war – oil, wreckage, and corpses – was strewn across local beaches.”

The insurmountable losses eventually prompted naval leadership in the United States to take action. Along with a convoy system being implemented in the shipping lanes off the Outer Banks, long-range aircraft patrols were organized and plans were made to deploy anti-submarine vessels in the region. Britain’s offers of assistance were also (finally) accepted.

Noting the increased resistance, Karl Dönitz withdrew the majority of his U-boats from the region and deployed them elsewhere.

**More from us:** [There Are Three U-boats Entombed Beneath a Parking Lot in Germany’s Second-Largest City](https://www.warhistoryonline.com/ships/elbe-ii-u-boats.html)

Along with the aforementioned loss of ships, 5,100 people lost their lives: 5,000 on the Allied side and 100 Germans. On top of the three U-boats that were sunk, another 40 were captured.
